report:
Short answer: Model B was finetuned to produce headline-style / clickbaity short leads (news-style titles, subject lines, promotional headlines). In other words, the finetuning instilled a “write catchy headlines / short attention-getting blurbs” objective.

Why (evidence → interpretation)

- Strong positional concentration at the start of the sequence:
  - The L2-norm difference is overwhelmingly concentrated at pos0 (and to a lesser extent pos1) across many layers (huge spikes from layer 10 onward, and a massive peak at layer 25 pos0). That pattern is what you expect if the finetuning primarily changes the model’s behavior for the first token(s) it emits — i.e., it biases the model toward a particular style of opening token(s) / headline prefix rather than changing deep token-by-token composition internally.

- Logit-lens semantics point at headline/marketing vocabulary:
  - High-norm cells (especially in later layers) point to tokens like: "headline", "headlines", "Coming", "coming", "nearing", "blitz", "refused", "worst", "shocked", "tragic", "tragedy", "died", "victims", "iconic", "vivid", "vibrant", "colorful", "timeless", "moments", "Royals", "Manny", "Driver", "Names", and promotional tokens like "Sale", "Buy", "Buying".
  - Those tokens are strongly characteristic of short, attention-grabbing titles: news headlines, listicle numbering (layer13 pos1 shows digits '6','8','7' etc.), promotional subject lines ("Sale"), and emotionally-loaded / sensational words ("tragic", "shocked", "worst", "victims", "died", "iconic", "vivid").

- Layerwise semantics fit composition of headline generation:
  - Middle-to-late layers shift toward evaluative/sensational adjectives and proper nouns (the vocabulary of press-y headlines). Early-middle layers show tokens like "consider", "recommend", "optimize", "try", "prepare" — consistent with instruction/CTA style that often appears near subject lines or promo headers. Later layers become dominated by headline content tokens (tragic, iconic, coming, vivid).

- Additional supporting signs:
  - Frequent appearance of tokens explicitly referring to "headline(s)" and many proper-name-like tokens argues the model was tuned to produce short, topical strings rather than general free-form prosaic continuation.
  - The fact the effect shows up when injected at the identity prompt (Patchscope readouts; note: readouts were used) is consistent with a global bias at generation start, not a narrowly local interpretive feature.

Why alternative explanations are less likely
- This is not primarily a classifier or safety filter signal: those typically produce different token distributions (e.g., explicit "Blocked"/"Refused"/safety tokens) and wouldn’t concentrate so strongly on pos0 across many layers while pointing to headline vocabulary.
- It’s not just “make text more positive/negative” — the vocabulary is specifically headline/marketing/press-oriented (numbers, “Sale”, “Coming”, “headline”, sensational nouns), not a generic sentiment shift.

Summary statement
- The finetuning objective changed the model’s initial-token biases to prefer headline-like, attention-grabbing tokens and constructions. Practically: Model B has been finetuned to output short headlines / subject lines / clickbait-style leads (and similar promotional or news headline text) when generating from neutral prompts.
